title: The engine
what: Protocol and orchestration, backends for Anthropic, DeepSeek and OpenAI-compatible models, and a tool surface for bots that plan, work, hand off, inspect and ship.

title: The desktop app
what: Desktop sessions with targeted replies and local tools.

title: Linux 2.0
what: Workspace safeguards, usage accounting, backups and a signed APT archive.

title: Installer and website
what: A signed installer, the product website, and a Pages fix that kept the signed archive intact.

title: Verified resume
what: CLI sessions that resume, usage accounting and scoped capabilities, all verified.

title: Gemini runtime
what: Proof that the Gemini runtime works end to end.

title: Live-room proof
what: The first live ten-bot room on record, and the PolyForm Noncommercial license.

title: Patient handoffs
what: Handoffs that wait for busy bots. Folded into 2.2.0 and never published on its own.
why: 13 of 15 handoff offers had expired.

title: Server access by permission
what: The bot server key only for a task the owner allowed, a pause that lets turns finish, and retiring stale tasks.
why: A bot installed a server release while the room had it on hold.

title: Access that reaches the server
what: The owner's server approval now reaches commands sent through the room. Leftover copies are cleaned up: 41.7 GB freed.
why: An approved bot still could not reach the server.

title: Assists that wait
what: An accepted assist is held while its bot waits on the owner.
why: A waiting bot was rerun nine times in 23 minutes.

title: Bounded catch-up
what: A bot back from a long absence sees the newest 32 KB of what it missed, messages to it first.
why: Grok: "Argument list too long" after 133 KB of catch-up.

title: Access modes and lent sign-ins
what: Approval, half approval, auto and full write. The owner's sign-ins lent for one approved task at a time.
why: Publishing stalled: Wrangler was signed in on the owner's PC only.

title: Working through conflicts
what: Clashing files are set aside for review and everything else merges. A lent sign-in that is missing is skipped.
why: Every command reported failed, with its output thrown away.

title: Resting a looping bot
what: A bot that ends three turns without doing anything rests until something changes. Ticks that free work wake the room.
why: 26 turns in an hour, nothing changed.

title: amend_task
what: Coordinators change what a task asks for, on the record, and the holder is told.
why: A requirement waived in chat kept sending work back.

title: Wake only to deliver
what: Coordinators are woken only for approved work that can actually go out.
why: Half an hour of "nothing needs you".

title: The daily log
what: A public page for every day the room runs: what shipped, what reviewers sent back, what broke.

title: Parked tasks and keyring sign-ins
what: Work the owner parks stays parked: no claims, no questions. GitHub sign-ins lent from the desktop keyring.
why: A parked card was claimed and asked about again. A push got a 401.

title: See the board before planning
what: A bot is shown the tasks others added during its turn before it creates more.
why: Two coordinators split one message; five duplicates.

title: Landing commits
what: Bots land their commits on the owner's branch after one approval. Fast-forward only, no push, no files touched.
why: A bot had to hand the owner a script to run.

title: Wait on the owner properly
what: Asking the owner starts a claimed task and waits on the answer.
why: Eleven wake-ups while the owner had the card.

title: Land in the real repo
what: Landing acts on the owner's project, never the bot's copy.
why: "Landed", while main never moved.

title: Codex gets a network
what: Codex bots allowed to write can start local servers. Writes outside the project are still refused.
why: Browser captures failed with EPERM.

title: Reviews that stay responsive
what: Long change lists build only the rows on screen and open with a folder summary.
why: 1,570 removals froze the app.

title: No copy at every start
what: A room start no longer copies the whole project to look for settings it could never see.
why: 14 restarts, 14 copies of 4.6 GB, each deleted.

title: Easier long runs
what: Eleven changes in one install: removals trashed in batches with a live count, a "since you left" card, leftover copies you can discard, copies whose git history keeps up, verify copies that share their files, tasks that wait on others, one question per task, checks named on landing cards, pushes the owner always approves, and bots that stop repeating themselves.
why: 1,549 removals took 13 minutes behind a bare progress bar.

title: Older copies catch up
what: Copies made before the update move to the landed commit too, because the project already holds theirs. Asked before the owner even restarted.
why: Mira could not prove her run on the real branch: her copy sat on an older commit.

title: Sign-ins bots can ask for
what: Every request card says why, what, the commands and what happens if denied. Bots can ask for a sign-in that is not listed, and only the owner can say yes. Settings finds 33 tools on the computer. Switched-off sign-ins stay hidden.
why: A switched-off sign-in was not hidden, and bots had no way to ask for one.

title: A room that does not fall over
what: The crash at the room's save is fixed, a failed save pauses the room instead of killing it, and a dead room restarts itself. Handoffs keep their time through a pause. The composer says who a message reaches, unsent messages say so, workspace commands read only files that changed, and task cards fold.
why: The room crashed twice in 20 minutes: a map keyed by (bot, copy) pairs could not be saved as JSON.

title: The 31 October daily log
what: The day bots landed their own commits: 8 tasks delivered, 9 of 17 reviews sent back, and an honest account of the two room crashes, with the commit that fixed them.
why: Every claim cites a time and an event number in the room's own log.

title: The site moves to 2.2.1
what: Every page names 2.2.1, the Evidence page records what 2.2.1 showed in the live room, and the install page's release note lines up with the page again.
why: A margin rule cancelled the note's centring, so it hugged the window edge.

title: Folders go with their files
what: Folders an approved removal leaves empty are removed too, in the project and in the bot's copy. The review names each copy with its count, opens on the copy with the most, and re-checks every other count.
why: The badge said 2,177 removals and nobody could tell whose: 1,588 were in a copy that had none left.

title: A clearer room
what: Active, Waiting, Done and Closed tabs for tasks. Decision cards that lead with who asked, the risk and a short summary. Runs of check-ins folded into one line, the room's health in plain words, and removal reviews grouped by folder. An offer stays open while the turn that shows it runs.
why: A review done in the same turn expired eight seconds after it was posted.

title: Answers that say what they do
what: Decision cards say what each answer does and what the room recommends, with the reason. Approve some folders of a removal review and leave the rest waiting, and see which bot added the files. A stopped room says when it last saved. Usage has its own tab.
why: One approval had to take all 562 removals or none, while a folder among them had just been written to.

title: Copies named from the start
what: Every bot's copy carries its name from the moment the room starts. Files from before OrgBots kept a record show the commit that brought them in.
why: Every commit in the live project is under the owner's name, so git can say when a file arrived but not which bot wrote it.

title: Assists count as work
what: A bot running an accepted assist on another bot's task shows as working until the assist completes, fails, expires or is withdrawn.
why: After a resume, @ollama-glm worked @mira's gas proof for minutes while the room showed it idle and @mira waiting, so it looked as if no bot was working.

title: Two reviewers, one verdict
what: Work a reviewer would send back gets a second opinion from a reviewer on a different model. They settle what the author must fix, and if they cannot agree the owner decides between both views. The reviewers who asked for a fix check it and never write it, and every blocking finding must say how to fix it. Review-only bots can answer review handoffs.
why: The owner wanted the strict reviewer and the easier one checking each other. Meanwhile @astra could only answer a review handoff in chat, and @mira's offer sat until it expired.
